narrative: The model estimates a 10% chance that you will fail your final year. That is a low risk, not a certainty, but in this process any flagged chance of failing makes remedial courses obligatory. The estimate is driven most strongly by your record of past class failures, then by your reason for choosing this school, and then by your weekly study time. Importantly, all three top signals push your risk downward rather than upward. You have no past class failures, which matches the average among students who passed and is a strong protective sign. Choosing the school for its reputation also lowers your predicted risk compared with choosing it for the course, proximity to home, or other reasons. Studying five to ten hours per week is also protective: only about one in five passing students reports that much, while most study only two to five hours, so your effort is above the norm. To improve further, keep your study routine steady, attend every class, and seek help early in any subject where you feel behind. Because your risk is already low, the remedial courses should be treated as preventive support rather than proof that failure is likely.
